hints: Focus on how first ionisation energy changes across Period 3, remembering there are two famous dips where the trend does not rise smoothly.
Check each trio and ask which middle element could be higher than both neighbours, this only happens at Mg and at P.
Now use melting point to decide between those two survivors, recall which element in Period 3 has the giant covalent high melting point and which are low melting simple molecules.
walkthrough:
**Recall the ionisation energy trend**

Think of first ionisation energy as how hard it is to pull off the outer electron. Across Period 3 it generally increases, but there are two drops.

General rise with dips: $$\text{Mg} > \text{Al} \text{ and } \text{P} > \text{S}$$

**Test which Y can be the highest**

For Y to be highest, it must sit on a peak just before a dip. That points to $\text{Mg}$ (higher than $\text{Na}$ and $\text{Al}$) and to $\text{P}$ (higher than $\text{Si}$ and $\text{S}$).

So only Na-Mg-Al and Si-P-S survive the first clue.

**Use melting point to choose**

Now think about structure. $\text{Si}$ is giant covalent with a very high melting point, while $\text{P}$ and $\text{S}$ are simple molecular solids with very low melting points.

In Si-P-S, $\text{P}$ ($44^{\circ}\text{C}$ white phosphorus) melts lower than $\text{S}$ ($115^{\circ}\text{C}$) and far lower than $\text{Si}$ ($1414^{\circ}\text{C}$), so Y is the lowest. In Na-Mg-Al, $\text{Na}$ is the lowest, not $\text{Mg}$, so that trio fails.

options.A: Na, Mg, Al fits the ionisation part because Mg (738 kJ/mol) is higher than Na and Al, but it fails on melting point. Na has the lowest melting point (about 98 C) due to weak metallic bonding, not Mg, so Y is not the lowest.
options.B: Mg, Al, Si fails on ionisation energy. Si has the highest first ionisation energy of the three (about 787 kJ/mol), not Al (about 578 kJ/mol), because Al is the dip after Mg. So Y is not the highest.
options.C: Al, Si, P fails on ionisation energy. P has the highest first ionisation energy (about 1012 kJ/mol) due to the steady rise from Al to P, not Si. So the middle element Si is not the highest.
options.D: Si, P, S fits both clues perfectly. For ionisation, P (about 1012 kJ/mol) is higher than Si (about 787 kJ/mol) and higher than S (about 1000 kJ/mol) because S is the dip due to spin-pair repulsion in the 3p orbital. For melting, P is simple molecular with the lowest melting point of the three, well below giant covalent Si and below S.
